title: Trigonometric Laws: Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
learningObjective: Use the law of sines and/or the law of cosines to solve non-right triangles.

faqs.question: What is the Law of Sines, and what does it actually say?
faqs.answer:
The Law of Sines says that in any triangle — right or not — the ratio of a side's length to the sine of its opposite angle is the same for all three sides.
Formula

\[ \dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} \]

You only ever need to set ONE fraction equal to another — not all three at once.

Each side is paired with the angle directly across from it — same color: side a ↔ angle A, side b ↔ angle B, side c ↔ angle C. The Law of Sines says each pair has the same ratio.

faqs.question: When can I use the Law of Sines to solve a triangle?
faqs.answer: The Law of Sines works whenever you have a complete opposite pair (an angle and the side directly across from it) plus one more piece of information. That covers AAS (two angles and a side across from one of them), ASA (two angles and the side between them: subtract from 180° to get the third angle, which pairs with the given side), and SSA (two sides and an angle that is not between them), though SSA comes with a complication of its own (faq-5).

faqs.question: What is the Law of Cosines, and how is it different from the Pythagorean Theorem?
faqs.answer:
The Law of Cosines relates all three sides of ANY triangle to the cosine of one included angle — it's a generalized version of the Pythagorean Theorem that works even when there's no right angle.
Formula

\[ a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A \]

If angle A happens to be 90°, then \( \cos A = 0 \), and the whole last term disappears — leaving exactly \( a^2=b^2+c^2 \), the Pythagorean Theorem. The Pythagorean Theorem is really just a special case of this more general law.

Law of Cosines setup: sides b and c (orange) are the two sides that form angle A, and side a (teal) is the side across from A: a² = b² + c² − 2bc·cos A.

faqs.question: When do I need the Law of Cosines instead of the Law of Sines?
faqs.answer: Use the Law of Cosines whenever you DON'T have a complete opposite pair (an angle and its directly-across side) to work with — specifically for SAS triangles (two sides and the included angle) and SSS triangles (all three sides, no angles at all). The Law of Sines simply has no way to get started in either of those situations.

faqs.question: What is the Ambiguous Case, and why does it only happen with the Law of Sines?
faqs.answer:
The Ambiguous Case happens specifically with SSA triangles (two sides and a non-included angle), where the given information can produce zero, one, or two valid triangles — not always exactly one. This happens because sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II (TR5), so when you solve for an angle using the Law of Sines, there are genuinely two different angle values that could both make the sine ratio true — and you have to check whether one, both, or neither actually forms a valid triangle. Finding an angle with the Law of Cosines doesn't have this problem: each cosine value between −1 and 1 matches exactly one angle between 0° and 180°. (The ambiguity comes from the SSA information itself. If you plug SSA information into the Law of Cosines, you get an equation that can also have zero, one, or two answers.) The TE5 CheckIt only gives SSA problems with one or two triangles; the no-triangle case is beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise.

Side a swings from C (dashed circle of radius a) and crosses the bottom line twice, so two different triangles fit the same given information.

faqs.question: What do AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, and SSS mean, and why does the letter order matter?
faqs.answer:
Each letter combination describes which three pieces of a triangle you're given, in the order you'd encounter them going around the triangle — A for a known angle, S for a known side. The ORDER matters because it tells you whether a given angle sits between two known sides or not.

The same triangle, five ways: orange marks the three pieces you're given (sides thick, angles as arcs). Which pieces you have — and in what order around the triangle — decides which law to use.

Summary

AAS / ASA — two angles + a side → Law of Sines (no ambiguity)

SSA — two sides + non-included angle → Law of Sines (Ambiguous Case!)

SAS — two sides + included angle → Law of Cosines

SSS — three sides, no angles → Law of Cosines

faqs.question: How do I solve a triangle when I'm given two angles and a side (AAS or ASA)?
faqs.answer:
Find the third angle first by subtracting the two known angles from 180°, then use the Law of Sines twice — once for each remaining missing side.

Triangle ABC, true to scale: angles A = 40° and C = 75° and side a = 12 are known (navy). Angle B and sides b and c (orange) are what we solve for.

Worked Example

Triangle ABC: \( A=40^\circ \), \( C=75^\circ \), \( a=12 \). Find B, b, and c.

\( B=180^\circ-40^\circ-75^\circ=65^\circ \)

\( \dfrac{12}{\sin 40^\circ}=\dfrac{b}{\sin 65^\circ} \) → \( b\approx 16.9 \)

\( \dfrac{12}{\sin 40^\circ}=\dfrac{c}{\sin 75^\circ} \) → \( c\approx 18.0 \)

faqs.question: How do I set up the Law of Sines proportion correctly?
faqs.answer:
Match each side with the angle DIRECTLY ACROSS from it — never a side with an adjacent angle. Write your proportion using only the one complete opposite pair you already know, plus the pair you're solving for.

Match across the triangle: the known pair is angle B with side b (navy). We're solving for side c, so its partner is the angle across from it, angle C (orange): b / sin B = c / sin C.

Worked Example

Known: angle \( B \) and its opposite side \( b \). Solving for side \( c \), opposite angle \( C \).

\( \dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C} \)

faqs.question: How do I know how many triangles exist in an SSA (Ambiguous Case) situation?
faqs.answer:
Solve for the unknown angle using the Law of Sines as usual, but check the result BEFORE moving on. If the sine value comes out greater than 1, no triangle exists at all — sine can never exceed 1 (TR5). If it's a valid sine value, you get one candidate angle immediately, and there's always a second candidate angle (180° minus the first) to check as well — see faq-11 for how to test whether that second candidate actually works. (If the sine is exactly 1, both candidates are \( 90° \): that is one candidate, not two.) (The height picture below assumes the given angle is acute, which it always is on the TE5 CheckIt. If the given angle is obtuse, there is one triangle when the side across from it is the longer of the two given sides, and none otherwise.)

For an acute given angle A, with side b and the swinging side a (dashed circle, radius a), compare a with the height h = b·sin A. The circle misses the bottom line (no triangle), touches it once (one right triangle), crosses it twice (two triangles), or crosses once beyond A, with its other crossing at A (when a = b) or behind A, which is not valid (one triangle). The TE5 CheckIt only uses the last two cases.

Worked Example — No Solution (beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise)

\( B=84^\circ \), \( a=18 \), \( b=9 \): \( \dfrac{18}{\sin A}=\dfrac{9}{\sin 84^\circ} \) → \( \sin A \approx 1.99 \)

Since sine can never exceed 1, no triangle exists.

faqs.question: How do I find both possible triangles when there are two solutions in the Ambiguous Case?
faqs.answer:
Solve for the first (acute) candidate angle using the inverse sine as usual, then find the second candidate by subtracting that result from 180°. Check that the second candidate is actually valid (faq-11), and if so, solve the REST of both triangles completely and separately — they'll have different remaining angles and sides.

Angle B = 35°, side a = 13, side b = 9, drawn to scale. Side b can swing to two spots on the bottom ray, A₁ (solid teal) and A₂ (dashed orange), giving two different triangles that share angle B and sides a and b.

Worked Example

\( B=35^\circ \), \( a=13 \), \( b=9 \): \( \sin A=\dfrac{13\sin 35^\circ}{9}\approx 0.8285 \), first candidate \( A\approx 55.9^\circ \), second candidate \( A\approx 124.1^\circ \).

\( 35^\circ+124.1^\circ=159.1^\circ<180^\circ \), so both are valid. Triangle 1: \( A\approx 55.9^\circ \), \( C\approx 89.1^\circ \), \( c\approx 15.7 \). Triangle 2: \( A\approx 124.1^\circ \), \( C\approx 20.9^\circ \), \( c\approx 5.6 \).

faqs.question: How do I know when a second candidate triangle from the Ambiguous Case is actually invalid?
faqs.answer:
Add the second candidate angle to the OTHER angle you already knew. If that sum is 180° or more, the third angle would have to be zero or negative — which is impossible — so that second triangle doesn't actually exist.

A triangle's angles must fit inside 180°. Once the two angles already add past 180°, there is no room for the third — so that candidate triangle is impossible.

Worked Example

Known angle \( A=35^\circ \), \( a=14 \), \( b=9 \): \( \sin B=\dfrac{9\sin 35^\circ}{14}\approx 0.3687 \), so \( B\approx 21.6^\circ \) and the second candidate is \( 180^\circ-21.6^\circ=158.4^\circ \).

\( 35^\circ+158.4^\circ=193.4^\circ \), already over 180° — this second triangle is impossible, so there is exactly one triangle.

faqs.question: How do I use the Law of Cosines to find a missing side when given two sides and the included angle (SAS)?
faqs.answer:
Plug the two known sides and the included angle directly into the Law of Cosines formula, matching the missing side to the angle between the two known sides.

SAS, true to scale: sides b = 14 and c = 7 and the angle between them, A = 70° (navy). The side across from A (orange) comes out to about 13.3.

Worked Example

Triangle ABC: \( A=70^\circ \), \( b=14 \), \( c=7 \). Find side a.

\( a^2=14^2+7^2-2(14)(7)\cos 70^\circ \)

\( a^2\approx 196+49-67.04\approx 177.96 \) → \( a\approx 13.3 \)

faqs.question: How do I use the Law of Cosines to find a missing angle when given all three sides (SSS)?
faqs.answer:
Rearrange the Law of Cosines to isolate the cosine term, plug in all three known sides, then apply the inverse cosine to solve for the angle itself.

SSS, true to scale: all three sides are known (navy) and angle C (orange), across from the longest side, is the unknown. It is wide: more than 90°.

Worked Example

Triangle with sides \( a=5 \), \( b=7 \), \( c=11 \). Find angle C (across from the longest side).

\( c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C \) → \( \cos C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab} \)

\( \cos C=\dfrac{25+49-121}{70}=\dfrac{-47}{70}\approx -0.6714 \) → \( C=\cos^{-1}(-0.6714)\approx 132.2^\circ \)

A negative cosine means C is obtuse, which fits: it is across from the longest side.

faqs.question: Once I've found one angle in an SSS or SAS triangle, how do I find the other two?
faqs.answer: Once you have at least one full opposite pair (an angle and its matching side), you can switch to the Law of Sines for a second angle, but only for an angle that cannot be obtuse. Choose the angle across from the shorter of the two remaining sides: it is not the largest angle, so it must be acute. The calculator's inverse sine only returns angles from 0° to 90°, so if you use it on an obtuse angle it reports 180° minus the real angle. Then find the third angle by subtracting the first two from 180°. If you would rather skip that check, use the Law of Cosines again: it gives the correct angle whether it is acute or obtuse.

faqs.question: How do I decide which law to use — Law of Sines or Law of Cosines — just by looking at what I'm given?
faqs.answer:
Check whether you have a complete opposite pair (an angle and the side directly across from it), or can make one. With two angles and any side (AAS or ASA), subtract from 180° to get the third angle; now the given side has its partner. With two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA), the given angle and the side across from it already form a pair. If you have a pair, use the Law of Sines (and for SSA, check for a second triangle). If you only have SAS or SSS information, there is no pair to start from, so start with the Law of Cosines.

A quick decision guide: the question is always whether you hold a complete opposite pair (an angle and the side directly across from it), or can make one by finding the third angle.

faqs.question: How does this section connect to TE4's right-triangle solving?
faqs.answer: TE4's tools — SOH-CAH-TOA and the Pythagorean Theorem — only work when a triangle has a right angle. This section extends triangle-solving to EVERY triangle, right or not, using two more general laws that still rely on the same underlying trig ratios TE4 introduced. In fact, faq-3 shows the Pythagorean Theorem is just the Law of Cosines with a 90° angle plugged in — TE4 was always a special case of what you're learning here.

faqs.question: How does the Ambiguous Case connect to TR5's quadrant sign ideas?
faqs.answer:
The entire reason the Ambiguous Case exists is TR5's observation that sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II — meaning two different angles between 0° and 180° can share the exact same sine value. Solving a triangle with the Law of Sines runs directly into that same ambiguity, which is why you always have to check both candidate angles rather than assuming there's only one answer.

On the unit circle, the angles B and 180° − B land at exactly the same height — so they have the same sine. When the Law of Sines hands you a sine value, both angles are candidates for the triangle.

faqs.question: Extension: Why do the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Surveying, navigation, and engineering all depend on solving triangles that aren't conveniently right triangles — measuring distances across terrain you can't directly walk across, calculating forces at odd angles, or triangulating a position using bearings to two known landmarks. These two laws are the standard tools for exactly that kind of real-world triangle, and they reappear constantly in physics and any field involving vectors or forces at an angle.

guided.title: Practice the Law of Sines for AAS/ASA
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve a triangle using the Law of Sines when I'm given two angles and a side. Give me a triangle like this and walk me through finding the third angle first, then using the Law of Sines twice to find the two missing sides. Give me more practice problems and check my work.

guided.title: Check the AI's two-triangle work
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing TE5 problems where I'm given two sides and an angle that is not between them, like the TE5 CheckIt. On the CheckIt the given angle is a multiple of 5 degrees and always acute, the sides are whole numbers, and there is always either one triangle or two (never zero). The letters may be shuffled, so the known side-and-opposite-angle pair might be c and C instead of a and A.

1. Give me one problem like that. To make it valid, pick the given angle from 10 to 50 degrees and the other given side from 9 to 15. For two triangles, make the side across from the given angle longer than (other side) times sin(given angle) but shorter than the other side. For one triangle, make it 2 to 10 longer than the other side. Don't tell me which kind it is, and don't solve it.
2. I'll solve it first: I'll say which law I used and why, find the second angle, test whether 180 degrees minus that angle also fits, and solve every triangle to the nearest tenth. Check my work one step at a time with questions, not answers.
3. Then give me a second problem of the other kind and show a full worked solution that contains exactly one deliberate mistake (for example: stopping after one triangle, pairing a side with the wrong angle, or using a value from one triangle in the other). Don't tell me where the mistake is.
4. I'll find the mistake, explain why it's wrong, and check it against my notes or the TE5 support page.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Three sides: find the widest angle first
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing TE5 triangles where I know all three sides. On the TE5 CheckIt, these triangles always have one wide angle (more than 110 degrees), and the other two angles can be very small.

1. Give me a triangle like that: pick two different whole numbers from 5 to 15, and make the third side either their sum minus 1 or their difference plus 1. Don't solve it.
2. I'll find the largest angle first with the law of cosines, then a second angle, then the third, rounding to the nearest tenth of a degree and keeping unrounded values in my calculator. Ask me why I started with the largest angle, and what the negative cosine tells me.
3. Then make a new triangle of the same kind and solve it yourself, but put exactly one deliberate mistake in your work. It could be a sign error in the cosine, the wrong side in the subtracted spot, rounding too early, or finding the wide angle with inverse sine. Don't tell me which.
4. I'll find the mistake, explain why it changes the answer, and check that your corrected angles add to 180 degrees (or 179.9 or 180.1 after rounding).

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Which law? (shuffled letters)
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing the first step of every TE5 problem: deciding whether to start with the law of sines or the law of cosines.

1. Give me 6 sets of givens written like the TE5 CheckIt ("In triangle ABC, ..."). Mix four kinds: three sides; two sides and the angle between them; two angles and a side; two sides and an angle that is not between them. Shuffle the letters so the pieces aren't always A, a, and b. Use whole-number sides from 5 to 15 and angles that are multiples of 5 degrees; two given angles must add to less than 170 degrees, and every set must make at least one real triangle. Don't label the kinds.
2. For each set, I'll name the kind (SSS, SAS, AAS, ASA, or SSA), say which law I'd start with, and give my reason in terms of whether I know (or can find) a side and the angle across from it. If I get one wrong, ask me one question about it instead of correcting me.
3. Then give me your own answers for 4 new sets, with exactly one deliberate mistake in a choice of law or a reason. Don't say which one.
4. I'll find it and check it against my notes.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Connect the Ambiguous Case to TR5
guided.prompt:
In TR5 I learned that sine is positive in Quadrants I and II. I want to see why that makes some TE5 triangles have two answers.

1. Ask me to solve sin(theta) = 0.7 for theta between 0 and 180 degrees, to the nearest tenth, and to say where both answers sit on the unit circle. Don't give me the answers first.
2. Then ask me to solve cos(theta) = -0.7 on the same interval and to explain why that equation has only one answer.
3. Next, make three short claims about triangles and these angles, with exactly one of them false on purpose. For example, claims about whether both angles from step 1 could be an angle of a triangle, what happens when one of them is added to a known 40 degree angle, or whether finding an angle with the law of cosines can give two answers. Don't tell me which claim is false.
4. I'll pick the false claim and check it against the unit circle and my notes.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 48^\circ\) and \(B = 71^\circ\). Find \(C\). Which side is the longest?[[graph:G1q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 48 degrees and B = 71 degrees. Find C. Which side is the longest?
stops.coldA: \(C = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 71^\circ = 61^\circ\). The largest angle is \(B = 71^\circ\), so the longest side is \(b\).[[graph:G1s]]
stops.solution: C = 180 - 48 - 71 = 61 degrees. The largest angle is B = 71, and the longest side is the one across from it: side b.
stops.mistake: Picking the side that touches the largest angle instead of the side across from it.
stops.again: \(A = 112^\circ\), \(C = 25^\circ\). Find \(B\). Which side is longest? Which is shortest?
stops.againA: \(B = 43^\circ\). Longest side \(a\) (across from \(112^\circ\)); shortest side \(c\) (across from \(25^\circ\)).
stops.reflect: How could "longest side across from largest angle" help you catch a wrong answer later?

stops.title: Calculator: degrees, inverse trig, and proportions
stops.target: In degree mode, solve a proportion by cross-multiplying, and undo \(\sin\) or \(\cos\) with \(\sin^{-1}\) or \(\cos^{-1}\).
stops.cold: (1) Solve \(\dfrac{x}{\sin 40^\circ} = \dfrac{12}{\sin 75^\circ}\) to the nearest tenth. (2) Find every angle \(\theta\) strictly between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) with \(\sin\theta = 0.8\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.coldPlain: (1) Solve x / sin 40 degrees = 12 / sin 75 degrees, to the nearest tenth. (2) Find every angle theta strictly between 0 and 180 degrees with sin theta = 0.8, to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.coldA: (1) \(x = \dfrac{12\sin 40^\circ}{\sin 75^\circ} \approx 8.0\). (2) \(\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.8) \approx 53.1^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ - 53.1^\circ \approx 126.9^\circ\). Both are possible triangle angles.
stops.solution: (1) Multiply both sides by sin 40: x = 12 sin 40 / sin 75, about 8.0. (2) theta = sin^(-1)(0.8), about 53.1 degrees. Sine is also positive in Quadrant II, so 180 - 53.1, about 126.9 degrees, has the same sine.
stops.mistake: Leaving the calculator in radian mode: 12 sin(40)/sin(75) comes out about -23.1, which cannot be a side length.
stops.againA: (1) \(x \approx 4.5\). (2) \(\cos^{-1}(-0.3) \approx 107.5^\circ\) (a negative cosine gives an obtuse angle).
stops.reflect: What is a quick way to check that your calculator is in degree mode before a quiz?

stops.title: Two angles can share a sine
stops.target: Between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), \(\sin\theta = \sin(180^\circ - \theta)\), so an equation \(\sin\theta = k\) with \(0 \lt k \lt 1\) has two answers. An equation \(\cos\theta = k\) with \(-1 \lt k \lt 1\) has exactly one.
stops.cold: For \(0^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ\): (1) solve \(\sin\theta = 0.6\); (2) solve \(\cos\theta = -0.6\). Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.coldPlain: For theta between 0 and 180 degrees: (1) solve sin theta = 0.6; (2) solve cos theta = -0.6. Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.solution: Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, so sin theta = 0.6 gives 36.9 degrees from the calculator and also 180 - 36.9 = 143.1 degrees. Cosine is negative only in Quadrant II on this interval, so cos theta = -0.6 gives only 126.9 degrees.
stops.mistake: Stopping at the calculator answer for sine and missing 180 - theta.
stops.reflect: Why might two different triangles have angles with the same sine? (This is exactly the "ambiguous case" coming up.)

stages.desc: Choose the law, use each law, then handle the ambiguous SSA case.

stops.title: Which law? Look for a matched pair
stops.target: Name what you are given (AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, SSS) and choose the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines, with a reason.
stops.cold: Which law would you start with, and why? (1) \(A = 50^\circ, B = 75^\circ, c = 11\) (2) \(a = 7, b = 9, C = 52^\circ\) (3) \(a = 5, b = 7, c = 9\) (4) \(A = 25^\circ, a = 7, b = 13\)
stops.coldPlain: Which law would you start with, and why? (1) A = 50 degrees, B = 75 degrees, c = 11 (2) a = 7, b = 9, C = 52 degrees (3) a = 5, b = 7, c = 9 (4) A = 25 degrees, a = 7, b = 13
stops.coldA: (1) ASA: find \(C = 55^\circ\) first, then \(c\) and \(C\) are a matched pair, so Law of Sines. (2) SAS: \(C\) is between \(a\) and \(b\), no matched pair, so Law of Cosines. (3) SSS: no angles, so Law of Cosines. (4) SSA: \(a\) and \(A\) are a matched pair, so Law of Sines, and check for two triangles.
stops.solution: (1) ASA; the third angle C = 55 makes c and C a matched pair, so Law of Sines. (2) SAS; the given angle sits between the two given sides, so there is no matched pair: Law of Cosines. (3) SSS; no angles at all: Law of Cosines. (4) SSA; a and A are a matched pair, so Law of Sines, but this is the ambiguous case, so check for 0, 1, or 2 triangles.
stops.mistake: Choosing a law by memorized letter patterns without checking whether a side and its opposite angle are both known.
stops.again: (1) \(B = 15^\circ, C = 25^\circ, b = 6\) (2) \(b = 8, c = 11, A = 120^\circ\). On a CheckIt the letters may be shuffled, so read which angle is across from which side.
stops.againA: (1) AAS, \(b\) and \(B\) are a matched pair: Law of Sines. (2) SAS, \(A\) is between \(b\) and \(c\): Law of Cosines.
stops.reflect: In your own words, what is a "matched pair," and why does the Law of Sines need one?

stops.title: Law of Sines: AAS and ASA
stops.target: With two angles and a side, find the third angle, then use \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}\) for each missing side.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 50^\circ\), \(B = 75^\circ\), and \(c = 11\). Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).[[graph:T2q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 50 degrees, B = 75 degrees, and c = 11. Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: C = 180 - 50 - 75 = 55, so c = 11 and C = 55 are a matched pair. a = 11 sin 50 / sin 55, about 10.3. b = 11 sin 75 / sin 55, about 13.0. Check: the largest angle, B = 75, is across from the longest side, b.
stops.mistake: Trying to use the Law of Sines before finding C, so there is no complete ratio to set equal.
stops.againA: \(A = 140^\circ\), \(a = \dfrac{6\sin 140^\circ}{\sin 15^\circ} \approx 14.9\), \(c = \dfrac{6\sin 25^\circ}{\sin 15^\circ} \approx 9.8\). The obtuse angle \(A\) is across from the longest side \(a\).
stops.reflect: Why does AAS or ASA never give two different triangles?

stops.title: Law of Cosines: SAS
stops.target: With two sides and the angle between them, find the third side with \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\). Then find an angle that is not across from the longest side, and finish with the angle sum.
stops.explain:
The Law of Cosines is the Pythagorean Theorem with a correction term for angles that are not \(90^\circ\).

[[graph:PYTH]]
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(a = 7\), \(b = 9\), and \(C = 52^\circ\). Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).[[graph:T3q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 9, and C = 52 degrees. Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: c^2 = 49 + 81 - 126 cos 52, about 52.43, so c is about 7.2. a = 7 is not the longest side, so A is acute and the Law of Sines is safe: sin A = 7 sin 52 / c, using the unrounded c (about 7.2406), so A is about 49.6. (Dividing by the rounded 7.2 gives 50.0, which is off.) B = 180 - 52 - 49.6, about 78.4. Keep unrounded values in the calculator between steps.
stops.mistake: Computing (49 + 81 - 126) cos 52 instead of 49 + 81 - (126 cos 52): multiply 2ab by cos C before subtracting.
stops.stretch: In the last problem, why would it be risky to find the \(120^\circ\) angle with the Law of Sines if it had not been given?
stops.stretchA: For a positive input, \(\sin^{-1}\) returns an angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). Since \(\sin 120^\circ = \sin 60^\circ\), the calculator would report \(60^\circ\). Find the largest angle with the Law of Cosines or the angle sum.
stops.reflect: What does the sign of cos C tell you about the side across from C?

stops.title: Law of Cosines: SSS
stops.target: With three sides, find the largest angle first with \(\cos C = \dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\) (a negative value means obtuse), then the rest.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(a = 5\), \(b = 7\), \(c = 9\). Solve the triangle (round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree).[[graph:T4q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, a = 5, b = 7, c = 9. Solve the triangle (round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: The longest side is c = 9, so find C first: cos C = (25 + 49 - 81)/70 = -0.1, C about 95.7 degrees (obtuse). Then sin A = 5 sin C / 9 gives A about 33.6, and B = 180 - C - A, about 50.7.
stops.mistake: Putting the wrong side in the subtracted spot: the side across from the angle you want is the one subtracted.
stops.reflect: Why is "largest angle first" a good habit when you will use the Law of Sines afterward?

stops.title: SSA: zero, one, or two triangles?
stops.target: Given \(A\), \(a\), and \(b\): find \(\sin B = \dfrac{b\sin A}{a}\). If it is more than 1, there is no triangle (beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise). Otherwise test both \(B\) and \(180^\circ - B\): each one counts only if \(A\) plus that angle is less than \(180^\circ\). (If the sine is exactly 1, there is only one candidate, \(90^\circ\); this is also beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise.)
stops.explain:
Side \(a\) hangs from \(C\) like a gate. It can swing to land on the base in two places, in one place, or not reach at all.

[[graph:SW]]
stops.cold: How many triangles? (1) \(A = 25^\circ, a = 7, b = 13\) (2) \(A = 45^\circ, a = 13, b = 8\) (3) \(A = 40^\circ, a = 4, b = 10\) (beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise: CheckIt always has at least one triangle)
stops.coldPlain: How many triangles? (1) A = 25 degrees, a = 7, b = 13 (2) A = 45 degrees, a = 13, b = 8 (3) A = 40 degrees, a = 4, b = 10
stops.solution: (1) sin B = 13 sin 25 / 7, about 0.7849: B is about 51.7 or 128.3, and 25 + 128.3 < 180, so two triangles. (2) sin B = 8 sin 45 / 13, about 0.4351: B is about 25.8 or 154.2, but 45 + 154.2 > 180, so one triangle. (3) sin B = 10 sin 40 / 4, about 1.607, more than 1, so no triangle.
stops.mistake: Writing down only the calculator angle and never testing 180 - B.
stops.again: (1) \(B = 20^\circ, b = 9, c = 14\) (letters shuffled: find the matched pair first) (2) \(A = 110^\circ, a = 9, b = 6\) (beyond the TE5 CheckIt exercise: CheckIt\'s given angle is always acute)
stops.againA: (1) The matched pair is \(b\) and \(B\): \(\sin C = \dfrac{14\sin 20^\circ}{9} \approx 0.5320\), \(C \approx 32.1^\circ\) or \(147.9^\circ\); \(20^\circ + 147.9^\circ < 180^\circ\), so both work: two triangles. (2) \(\sin B \approx 0.6265\), \(B \approx 38.8^\circ\) works, \(141.2^\circ\) does not (\(110^\circ + 141.2^\circ > 180^\circ\)): one triangle.
stops.reflect: Use the gate picture: why does a short side a sometimes give two triangles and sometimes none?

stops.title: SSA: solve both triangles
stops.target: When there are two triangles, finish each one separately: \(C = 180^\circ - A - B\), then \(c = \dfrac{a\sin C}{\sin A}\). On a CheckIt the letters may be shuffled; use whichever side and opposite angle you were given.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 25^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(b = 13\). Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth). Show that you checked for a second triangle, and give both if there are two.
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 25 degrees, a = 7, and b = 13. Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth). Show that you checked for a second triangle, and give both if there are two.
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: sin B = 13 sin 25 / 7, about 0.7849, so B1 is about 51.7 and B2 = 180 - 51.7, about 128.3; both fit with A = 25 (25 + 128.3 < 180). Triangle 1: C about 103.3, c = 7 sin C / sin 25, about 16.1. Triangle 2: C about 26.7, c about 7.4.
stops.mistake: Mixing the two triangles, for example using C from triangle 1 to find c in triangle 2.
stops.again: \(B = 20^\circ\), \(b = 9\), \(c = 14\). Solve the triangle. (The letters are shuffled: the matched pair is \(b\) and \(B\).)
stops.reflect: How would you show a grader that you checked for a second triangle, even when there is only one?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE5 CheckIt: one Law of Cosines triangle, one Law of Sines triangle, and one that may have two solutions.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Solve non-right triangles: state which law you used and why, and check for a second triangle when the case is SSA.
stops.cold:
Solve each triangle. State whether you used the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines and explain your choice. If there may be two solutions, show that you checked and give both when appropriate. Round to the nearest tenth.
(1) \(a = 10\), \(c = 14\), and \(B = 35^\circ\).
(2) \(A = 55^\circ\), \(C = 60^\circ\), and \(b = 12\).
(3) \(C = 40^\circ\), \(c = 7\), and \(a = 10\).
stops.coldPlain: Solve each triangle, state which law and why, and check for two solutions. (1) a = 10, c = 14, B = 35 degrees. (2) A = 55 degrees, C = 60 degrees, b = 12. (3) C = 40 degrees, c = 7, a = 10. Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.coldA: (1) Law of Cosines (SAS): \(b \approx 8.2\), \(A \approx 44.6^\circ\), \(C \approx 100.4^\circ\).[[graph:SF1]](2) Law of Sines (ASA): \(B = 65^\circ\), \(a \approx 10.8\), \(c \approx 11.5\).[[graph:SF2]](3) Law of Sines (SSA), two triangles: \(A \approx 66.7^\circ\), \(B \approx 73.3^\circ\), \(b \approx 10.4\); or \(A \approx 113.3^\circ\), \(B \approx 26.7^\circ\), \(b \approx 4.9\).[[graph:SF3]][[graph:SWF]]
stops.solution: (1) SAS, B is between a and c: b^2 = 100 + 196 - 280 cos 35, b about 8.2; sin A = 10 sin 35 / b (unrounded b, about 8.163), A about 44.6; C about 100.4. (2) ASA: B = 65, a = 12 sin 55 / sin 65, about 10.8; c = 12 sin 60 / sin 65, about 11.5. (3) SSA, c and C are a matched pair: sin A = 10 sin 40 / 7, about 0.9183, so A is about 66.7 or 113.3; 40 + 113.3 < 180, so two triangles: B about 73.3 with b about 10.4, or B about 26.7 with b about 4.9.
stops.mistake: In (3), reading the letters as if they were A, a, b: here the matched pair is c and C, and the angle to solve for is A.
stops.againA: (1) Law of Cosines: \(C \approx 88.0^\circ\), \(A \approx 35.7^\circ\), \(B \approx 56.4^\circ\) (Keep unrounded values: if you use the rounded 88.0° and 35.7°, the angle sum gives 56.3°. CheckIt finds each angle on its own, so its three rounded angles can add to 180.1°.) (2) Law of Sines: \(C = 45^\circ\), \(b \approx 17.8\), \(c \approx 13.4\). (3) Law of Sines: \(\sin A \approx 0.5472\), \(A \approx 33.2^\circ\) (the other option, \(146.8^\circ\), is too big with \(50^\circ\)): one triangle, \(C \approx 96.8^\circ\), \(c \approx 18.1\).
stops.reflect: Which part of TE5 still feels shaky: choosing the law, the Law of Cosines arithmetic, or the ambiguous case?
